ruledOut: Lifting openhuman code directly under GPL-3.0
Copying OpenMausBot enterprise/ code outside the Apache-2.0 grant
Adopting OpenBot Kubernetes charts or the managed-upgrade agent for a small team

label: OpenBot ships as one container carrying the app, API and Chromium, with external or embedded PostgreSQL, so a small team can run the whole product on one host without a cluster.

OpenBot's supervisor gives each person or isolated bot its own container; without it every bot shares one computer, which the deployment doc calls fine for one team trusting its bots and explicitly not fine as a tenant boundary.

Kubernetes is a second deployment shape with two Helm charts, a management agent, release-manifest promotion and GitOps output, existing to give each person a computer and scale the API apart from browsers; a small team needs neither.

Managed upgrades are a fleet feature: a management agent heartbeats to CopilotKit, Flux installs named releases in a maintenance window, and every migrating upgrade needs a verified backup; a small team can upgrade by hand.
The team edition adds one Everyone admin scope above Every Bot and This Bot, with admin pages for the eight primitives plus vault and team; a few people on one machine do not need that policy layer.
Mobile is a separate Expo/React Native app with a deliberately limited launch scope and no Computer screen, so terminal-first parity does not need it.

License matrix: OpenBot, OpenGhost and Hermes Muse are MIT; OpenMausBot, Rakazo, Turnstone and Buzz are Apache-2.0; openhuman is GPL-3.0; OpenMausBot's Apache grant excludes enterprise/, which is source-available under a separate enterprise license.

Directly liftable routine code exists in permissive repositories: OpenBot plan.ts and routine-firing.ts (MIT), OpenMausBot routine-schedules.ts, routine-cron-text.ts and routine-wake-retry.ts (Apache-2.0), and Rakazo packages/core/src/routines/schedule.ts (Apache-2.0).

Other liftable pieces target the other parts: OpenGhost's hook-compatible rules engine for approvals (MIT), Hermes Muse's owned-job table and watch prompt for routines (MIT), and Turnstone's output-guard judge for activity and approval review (Apache-2.0).

Ranked build order: routine block and planner; approvals inbox and activity feed; terminal conversation with per-bot memory; memory and skill mapping; apps and secret vault; per-bot computer over worktrees; small-team sign-in and roles only on a shared host.
